title: How Much Is an ER Visit Without Insurance? 2026 Costs by Level
summary: How much is an ER visit without insurance? The facility fee alone has a median of about $224 to $1,537 by level. See what adds to the bill and how to lower it.
body_markdown:
If you go to the emergency room without health insurance, the bill depends on how serious your visit is coded, which hospital you use, and how many tests and treatments you receive. The hospital's facility fee for a mid-level visit has a median self-pay price of about **$645 to $1,050** , and the emergency physician, imaging, lab work, and any procedures are billed on top of that. Here's what an ER visit costs without insurance, how the bill is built, and what you can do about it.


## ER visit cost without insurance: quick answer


- **Facility fee only:** median self-pay prices range from about $224 for a Level 1 visit to about $1,537 for a Level 5 visit, across more than 3,000 U.S. hospitals, according to[SelfPayRates](https://selfpayrates.com/procedure/99284) , which compiles hospital price transparency files.
- **Physician fees:** the emergency doctor's charges are billed separately, and so are radiologists and any specialists.
- **Add-ons:** imaging, lab tests, medications, and procedures such as stitches can cost more than the facility fee itself.
- **For comparison:** the average emergency department visit for people with large-employer insurance cost $2,453 in total (2019 data), according to the[Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/emergency-department-visits-exceed-affordability-thresholds-for-many-consumers-with-private-insurance/) .


Uninsured patients are usually billed as "self-pay." Many hospitals publish a discounted cash price for self-pay patients, but if you don't ask, you may first receive a bill based on the hospital's full list prices (its chargemaster).


## How ER billing works: facility, physician, and add-on charges


An emergency room visit produces several bills stacked together, which is why the final cost often surprises people. Knowing how ER billing works makes the bill easier to check.


- **Facility fee:** what the hospital charges for the emergency room itself: the space, equipment, and nursing staff. It is set mainly by the visit level (see below).
- **Physician and clinician fees:** the emergency medicine group bills for the doctor's evaluation. Radiologists who read your scans and specialists who consult each send their own charges.
- **Imaging:** X-rays, CT scans, and ultrasounds. For privately insured patients, imaging added an average of $483 to an emergency department visit, about 19% of the total ([Peterson-KFF](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/emergency-department-visits-exceed-affordability-thresholds-for-many-consumers-with-private-insurance/) ).
- **Lab tests:** blood panels, urinalysis, and cultures.
- **Medications and supplies:** IV fluids, medicines given in the ER, dressings, and splints.
- **Procedures:** stitches, splinting, or setting a fracture.


Facility fees have grown much faster than physician fees. For privately insured patients, the average emergency department facility fee for the visit itself was $713 in 2021, compared with $321 for the professional fee, according to a[Peterson-KFF analysis](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/how-do-facility-fees-contribute-to-rising-emergency-department-costs/) .


## Emergency room cost by visit level (CPT 99281 to 99285)


Emergency visits are coded at one of five levels, CPT 99281 through 99285, based on how complex the visit is and how much decision-making it required. The level drives the facility fee. These are median self-pay prices for the hospital facility fee only, from[SelfPayRates](https://selfpayrates.com/) :


**Visit level**


**CPT code**


**Median self-pay facility fee**


Level 1 (minor problem)


99281


$224


Level 2 (low complexity)


99282


$390


Level 3 (moderate)


99283


$645


Level 4 (moderate to high)


99284


$1,047


Level 5 (high complexity)


99285


$1,537


Prices vary widely around those medians. For a Level 4 visit, most hospitals charge between about $426 and $3,308 for the facility fee alone, and state medians run from about $418 in Louisiana to about $3,729 in Utah ([SelfPayRates](https://selfpayrates.com/procedure/99284) ). For a Level 3 visit, the middle half of hospitals charge between about $271 and $1,918 ([SelfPayRates](https://selfpayrates.com/procedure/99283) ).


Higher-level coding has become more common: the share of emergency department facility claims billed at the highest level rose from 5% to 20% between 2004 and 2021 for privately insured patients ([Peterson-KFF](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/how-do-facility-fees-contribute-to-rising-emergency-department-costs/) ). If your bill is coded at Level 4 or 5 for what seemed like a simple problem, ask the billing department to explain the level and the documentation behind it.


## Average emergency room visit cost: what the whole visit adds up to


The total ER cost depends on what you're treated for. A visit for a minor cut that needs a few stitches involves far fewer services than a chest pain workup with an EKG, repeated blood tests, and imaging, or an evaluation for severe abdominal pain that includes a CT scan.


Data on privately insured patients shows how much the level matters. In 2019, the average total cost of an emergency department visit was $592 at Level 1 and $3,857 at Level 5, with an overall average of $2,453 ([Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/emergency-department-visits-exceed-affordability-thresholds-for-many-consumers-with-private-insurance/) ). These are amounts negotiated by insurers, not self-pay prices, but they give a sense of how quickly the add-ons stack up.


When it is medically safe, you can ask whether a test is needed now or whether it could be done later at an outpatient center. In a true emergency, speed and safety come first.


## ER visit costs vs. urgent care clinics and other options


For non-life-threatening conditions, urgent care usually costs much less than an emergency room visit. A standard self-pay urgent care visit typically costs about $150 to $280 for the evaluation before tests (see our guide to[urgent care cost without insurance](https://www.withflex.com/blog/urgent-care-cost-without-insurance) ), compared with a median ER facility fee of about $645 for a Level 3 visit before the physician fee.


Urgent care centers handle many minor issues, often with nurse practitioners or physician assistants on staff. Common reasons for an urgent care visit include:


- Minor cuts that need a few stitches
- Sprains and strains
- Ear infections, colds, and flu symptoms
- Urinary tract infections


For a non-urgent problem, a virtual visit or your primary care doctor may be an even lower-cost option, and they can tell you whether you need in-person medical care.


Some symptoms are considered life-threatening and need immediate attention from emergency services. Go to the emergency room or call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke symptoms (face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech), severe bleeding, a serious head injury, or a possible overdose. Never delay emergency care because of cost.


If you're taken to the ER by ambulance, that ride is billed separately. See our guide to[ambulance ride costs](https://www.withflex.com/blog/ambulance-ride-cost) .


## Your rights in the ER: EMTALA


The[Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA)](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/regulations-guidance/legislation/emergency-medical-treatment-labor-act) requires hospitals that participate in Medicare and have an emergency department to provide a medical screening exam to anyone who comes in asking for care, and to stabilize an emergency medical condition, regardless of insurance or ability to pay. Hospitals can't delay the screening exam to ask how you'll pay.


EMTALA guarantees access to emergency care, not free care. The hospital can still bill you afterward, so the steps below matter.


## Good faith estimates and surprise billing rules for uninsured patients


Under the No Surprises Act, people who are uninsured or not using insurance can get a[good faith estimate](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/know-your-rights/without-insurance) of expected charges for scheduled care, when it's booked at least 3 business days ahead. You won't get an estimate during emergency care.


That still matters after an ER visit: follow-up imaging, procedures, or specialist visits that you schedule are covered. If the final bill for that scheduled care is at least $400 more than the estimate, you can start a dispute within 120 days of getting the bill, according to CMS.


## How to read an itemized ER bill


The first statement you receive is often a summary. Ask the hospital for an itemized bill, which lists each charge with:


- The service description
- The date and quantity
- The billing code (CPT or HCPCS)
- The charge for each line


Check it against your discharge paperwork. Look for duplicate charges, services you didn't receive, wrong quantities, and a visit level that doesn't match what happened. Ask the billing office to explain vague lines such as "pharmacy" or "supplies," and get any corrections in writing.


## Ways to lower an ER bill without insurance


- **Ask for the self-pay price.** Under federal[hospital price transparency rules](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency) , hospitals must post their discounted cash prices. Ask the billing office whether that price was applied to your bill.
- **Apply for financial assistance or charity care.** Nonprofit hospitals must have a written[financial assistance policy](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/financial-assistance-policy-and-emergency-medical-care-policy-section-501r4) that covers emergency care, and patients who qualify can't be charged more than the amounts the hospital generally bills insured patients, under IRS rules. Many hospitals set eligibility for their financial assistance programs by comparing your income with the federal poverty level. Ask for the policy and the application, even if you've already received a bill.
- **Negotiate with the billing department.** Explain any financial hardship, and ask whether the hospital will accept a reduced amount, especially if you can pay a lump sum.
- **Set up a payment plan.** Most hospitals offer one for large bills. Ask for the longest no-interest plan available, and get the total, the monthly payment, and the terms in writing.


Contact the billing office early. Once an account goes to collections, you have fewer options.


## How health insurance changes the cost


With a health insurance plan, you pay the rate your health plan negotiated with the hospital, plus your share through your[deductible](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-deductible) ,[copay](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-copay) , and[coinsurance](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-coinsurance) , up to your plan's[out-of-pocket maximum](https://www.withflex.com/blog/deductible-vs-out-of-pocket-maximum) . Even then, ER visits can be expensive: privately insured patients paid $646 out of pocket on average for an emergency department visit in 2019 ([Peterson-KFF](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/emergency-department-visits-exceed-affordability-thresholds-for-many-consumers-with-private-insurance/) ).


If you're comparing plans, our guide to[how much health insurance costs per month](https://www.withflex.com/blog/health-insurance-cost-per-month) explains the trade-off between premiums and out-of-pocket costs. Many plans also list a set ER copay in their summary of benefits, so check yours before you need it.


Whether you can pay with an HSA or FSA depends on your plan, and[IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) describes which medical expenses qualify. Our guide to[HSAs and FSAs](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) explains how the two accounts work.
